chapter_summary:
Embarking on a game development project, whether solo or with a team, requires more than just creative vision; it demands structured management to transform ideas into a playable reality. Without effective project management, even the most brilliant concepts can falter due to disorganization, miscommunication, or unchecked scope. In the game industry, two primary methodologies often come into play: Waterfall and Agile. While Waterfall, a linear sequential design process, might be suitable for projects with extremely well-defined requirements and minimal expected changes, the dynamic and iterative nature of game development often makes Agile methodologies a far superior choice. Agile embraces flexibility, continuous iteration, and collaboration, allowing teams to adapt to evolving design needs, player feedback, and unforeseen technical challenges.

Within the Agile umbrella, Scrum is a particularly popular framework for game development. Scrum organizes work into short, fixed-length iterations called "sprints," typically lasting one to four weeks. Each sprint begins with a planning session where the team commits to delivering a set of features, known as "user stories," from a prioritized "product backlog." Daily "stand-up" meetings (or daily scrums) keep everyone aligned, allowing team members to quickly share progress, discuss blockers, and coordinate efforts. At the end of a sprint, the team demonstrates the completed work in a "sprint review" and reflects on their process in a "sprint retrospective" to identify areas for improvement. This iterative cycle of planning, execution, review, and adaptation is crucial for managing the inherent uncertainties of game design and ensuring that the final product remains aligned with the core vision while being responsive to feedback.

Effective project management also hinges on clearly defined roles and responsibilities. While specific titles can vary between studios, common roles include the Producer, who oversees the entire project, manages budgets, schedules, and resources; the Lead Designer, who champions the game's vision and ensures design consistency; Lead Programmers, Artists, and Animators, who guide their respective teams; and Quality Assurance (QA) Leads, who ensure the game meets quality standards. As a game designer, you'll work closely with all these roles, translating design concepts into actionable tasks for programmers and artists, and collaborating with QA to refine gameplay. Understanding these interdependencies is vital for smooth communication and efficient workflow.

To keep track of tasks, progress, and deadlines, teams utilize various tools. For Scrum, digital boards like Jira, Trello, or Asana are invaluable. These tools allow teams to visualize their product backlog, sprint backlog, and the current status of tasks (e.g., "To Do," "In Progress," "Done"). For broader project scheduling, especially for major milestones, Gantt charts can provide a high-level overview of dependencies and timelines. Burndown charts, on the other hand, are excellent for tracking progress within a sprint, showing the remaining work versus time. These visual aids are not just for management; they empower the entire team to understand the project's health and contribute effectively.

Perhaps one of the most critical components of any collaborative game development pipeline is version control. Imagine multiple designers, artists, and programmers all working on the same game files simultaneously – without version control, chaos would ensue, leading to lost work, overwritten changes, and endless conflicts. Version control systems (VCS) like Git or Perforce allow teams to track every change made to every file, revert to previous versions, and, most importantly, merge changes from multiple contributors without destroying work. For instance, a designer might be tweaking level geometry while a programmer implements a new character ability, and an artist updates a texture. Git manages these parallel lines of development through branches, allowing each person to work independently and then integrate their changes safely.

Using Git, for example, a typical workflow involves creating a new "branch" for a specific feature or bug fix:
```bash
git checkout -b new-feature-branch
```
You then make your changes, add them to the staging area, and commit them:
```bash
git add .
git commit -m "Implemented new jump mechanic"
```
Once your feature is complete and tested, you push your branch to the central repository and create a "pull request" (or "merge request") for review:
```bash
git push origin new-feature-branch
```
After review, your changes are merged into the main development branch. This systematic approach prevents conflicts and ensures a complete history of the project. Common mistakes in version control include not committing frequently enough, committing broken code, or trying to resolve complex merge conflicts without understanding the underlying changes. Always communicate with your team about changes and pull requests to ensure a smooth integration process.

Finally, while tools and methodologies are important, the human element remains paramount. Scope creep, where new features are continuously added without adjusting timelines or resources, is a common pitfall that can derail projects. Clear communication, realistic goal setting, and strong leadership are essential to keep the project on track. Regularly reviewing the game's core vision and prioritizing features based on their impact and feasibility will help prevent over-scoping. Moreover, fostering a culture of open communication and psychological safety within the team ensures that issues are raised early and resolved collaboratively, rather than festering and becoming larger problems down the line.

screens.title: Game Project Management & Production Pipelines
screens.subtitle: Turn creative ideas into playable reality with structured workflows, clear roles, and version control

narration.text: Welcome. In this lesson you will learn how project management and production pipelines convert game ideas into playable builds without chaos. We'll compare the two common approaches used in studios, explain why iterative workflows are usually better for games, and show the practical tools teams use every day — from sprint boards to version control. You will see how clear roles like Producer, Lead Designer, and QA fit into the pipeline so work moves smoothly across artists, programmers, and designers. We'll also walk through simple artifacts you can create: a prioritized product backlog, a sprint board with To Do, In Progress, and Done, and a basic Git workflow for safe collaboration. Finally, we'll highlight common pitfalls such as scope creep and poor communication, and give straightforward mitigation strategies you can apply right away. By the end of these screens you'll be able to pick an appropriate methodology, draft a mini production schedule for a feature, and use version control practices to avoid overwriting teammates' work. Think of this as a practical playbook: the goal is reliable team coordination so creativity can scale. What would you change first on your last project after seeing these patterns?

keyIdea.title: Why management matters
keyIdea.text: Structured workflows keep creativity productive: methodologies, roles, tracking, and version control prevent lost work and uncontrolled scope.

screens.title: Waterfall vs Agile — choosing the right approach
screens.subtitle: Understand linear vs iterative trade-offs for game projects

narration.text: Game projects differ from many software projects because design evolves with playtesting and feedback. Waterfall is a linear sequence: requirements, design, implementation, testing, delivery. That structure can work when requirements are stable and assets are small, but in most game development work the rules, levels, and interactions change after testing. Agile — and Scrum in particular — embraces short iterations and frequent feedback. This matters because iterative cycles let you surface design problems early, adjust scope, and pivot without throwing away large amounts of work. A concrete example: if you design a combat system up front under Waterfall, you may discover after playtests that hit reactions need different timing, forcing large rework. Under Scrum, you build a minimal combat loop in the first sprint, test it, and refine mechanics in subsequent sprints. A common misconception is that Agile means no planning; in fact Agile requires continuous planning at multiple levels: product backlog grooming, sprint planning, and release planning. Another contrast is predictability: Waterfall can feel predictable on paper but brittle in reality; Agile gives less long-term predictability but much higher ability to respond to real play data. Key takeaway: choose Waterfall only for narrowly defined, low-change projects; prefer Agile for creative game work because it reduces wasted effort and improves alignment with player needs. Which approach would have saved time on a past project you've worked on?

keyIdea.title: Iterate to learn
keyIdea.text: Agile trade-offs favor adaptability and early feedback; prefer iterative workflows for most game development.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Waterfall vs Agile
Waterfall
Linear, phase-based
  • Plan once up front and follow phases sequentially.
  • Works when requirements are well-defined and unlikely to change.
  • Risk: late discovery of design problems leads to costly rework.
Misconception: Waterfall is always more predictable. It can be predictable only when scope is fixed and small.
Agile / Scrum
Iterative, feedback-driven
  • Work in short sprints, deliver playable increments, adapt based on feedback.
  • Supports changing design and rapid learning from playtests.
  • Requires continuous prioritization and strong collaboration.
Pro tip: Time-box experiments in early sprints to reduce risk and validate design quickly.

screens.title: Scrum fundamentals: sprints, roles, and ceremonies
screens.subtitle: How Scrum organizes iterative game development

narration.text: Scrum gives game teams a repeatable rhythm to plan, build, and review work. At its core are time-boxed sprints, typically one to four weeks long. Each sprint starts with sprint planning: the team selects user stories from the prioritized product backlog into a sprint backlog and commits to completing them. During the sprint, daily stand-ups keep everyone aligned and surface blockers quickly so the team can act. At the end, a sprint review demonstrates completed work to stakeholders for feedback, and a retrospective looks inward to improve the process. Concrete example: for a two-week sprint to add a crafting system, the team picks five user stories — recipe data, UI wireframe, combination logic, placeholder art, and QA tests — then breaks each into tasks with estimates. A misconception to avoid is treating the sprint backlog as a strict contract; it is a commitment but not a prison — truly blocking issues may require swapping tasks, while non-critical additions should return to the product backlog. Another important point is role clarity: the Product Owner prioritizes the backlog, the Scrum Master helps the team follow the process and remove blockers, and the team delivers increments. This framework helps teams iterate quickly while protecting focus and improving predictability week-to-week. What would your first sprint goal be for a small feature?

keyIdea.title: Sprint rhythm
keyIdea.text: Short, repeated sprints create predictable learning cycles: plan, build, review, and adapt.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Scrum Fundamentals
Process
Sprint Planning — select and estimate user stories
Daily Stand-up — sync and surface blockers
Sprint Review — demo playable increments
Retrospective — reflect and improve
Concrete example: Crafting System (2-week sprint)
  • User stories: combine two ingredients, view recipe, open UI, save crafted item.
  • Tasks: data structure design, UI wireframe, combination logic, placeholder art, QA tests.
  • Daily stand-up sample note: "Working on recipe data structure, need confirmation from designer; no blockers."
Check your understanding: How would you split a large story into smaller sprint-sized stories?

screens.title: Team roles and responsibilities
screens.subtitle: Who does what in a game production pipeline

narration.text: Clear roles prevent duplicated effort and ensure work flows between disciplines. In many studios the Producer oversees schedule, resources, and the relationship with stakeholders. The Lead Designer champions the game's vision and translates high-level design into user stories and implementation details. Lead Programmers, Lead Artists, and Lead Animators coordinate their teams to deliver technical systems and assets. QA Leads create test plans and drive bug reporting, working closely with developers to verify fixes. As a game designer you act as a bridge: you clarify feature intent for programmers and asset needs for artists, and you work with QA to iterate on issues discovered in playtests. A concrete mapping: when a new feature is added to the backlog, the Lead Designer writes the story and acceptance criteria, the Producer schedules it into a sprint or milestone, programmers estimate the implementation tasks, artists create placeholders that are refined over subsequent sprints, and QA prepares test cases. A common misconception is that titles fix responsibilities; instead, responsibilities must be communicated for each feature because teams and studios vary. Key takeaway: document who owns what for each user story and create a simple approval path so decisions don't stall the pipeline. Which ownership gap is most likely to cause delay on your team?

keyIdea.title: Ownership matters
keyIdea.text: Assign responsibility per story and keep handoffs explicit to avoid stalled tasks and miscommunication.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Team Roles
Role hierarchy
Producer
Manages schedule, resources, and stakeholder expectations.
Lead Designer
Defines vision, writes user stories, and sets acceptance criteria.
Lead Programmer / Lead Artist
Coordinate technical and art implementation and lead their teams.
QA Lead
Defines test plans, finds regressions, and verifies fixes.
Concrete scenario: handling a new feature
  • Designer: writes the user story and acceptance criteria.
  • Producer: schedules the work into an upcoming sprint and allocates effort.
  • Programmer/Artist: break story into tasks, estimate, and implement.
  • QA: defines tests, reports bugs, and verifies fixes before marking Done.
Tip: Add an explicit owner field to each backlog item so responsibility is always visible.

screens.title: Tools for tracking: boards, burndown, and Gantt
screens.subtitle: Pick the right visual aid for your planning horizon

narration.text: Visual tools give teams shared situational awareness. For day-to-day task flow, digital boards like Trello, Jira, or Asana represent the sprint backlog as cards in columns such as To Do, In Progress, and Done. This format helps the whole team see who is working on what and where blockers are. Burndown charts track remaining work versus time inside a sprint and are excellent for monitoring whether the team is on track to complete the committed stories. Gantt charts offer a higher-level timeline view of milestones and dependencies, useful for release planning and communicating with stakeholders. A concrete example: use a burndown chart during a two-week sprint to detect early whether scope needs trimming — if the line isn't dropping, investigate blockers immediately. A common misconception is that more tools equal better control; instead, choose one or two visuals and keep them updated. For example, keep the sprint board current for daily work, use a burndown for sprint health, and consult a Gantt only for cross-sprint dependencies. Key takeaway: align the tool to the question you need answered — status, progress, or timeline — and teach the team to update artifacts daily so they reflect reality. Which visual would you start with for your next sprint?

keyIdea.title: Use visuals strategically
keyIdea.text: Boards for daily flow, burndown for sprint health, Gantt for milestones — pick the right chart for the question.

Boards

Boards visualize current work and are updated continuously. They surface blockers and show ownership at a glance.
Burndown Chart
Tracks remaining story points over sprint time to monitor progress.
Gantt Overview
Shows milestones and dependencies across sprints for release planning.
Practical tip: update the board daily, check the burndown mid-sprint, and only update Gantt when milestones change.

screens.title: Version Control: why it's essential
screens.subtitle: Protecting work when multiple people modify the same files

narration.text: Version control systems are the backbone of collaborative game development. They track every change to files, make it possible to revert to previous versions, and allow multiple contributors to work in parallel without destroying each other's edits. Imagine three people editing the same scene asset or script at once — without a VCS you risk lost work and file conflicts. Tools like Git provide distributed branching models that let each contributor work on an isolated branch, while centralized systems like Perforce are common in larger studios that handle large binary assets. A concrete example: a designer creates a feature branch for a new jump mechanic and commits incremental changes. A programmer and an artist can work in their own branches; later these branches are merged into the mainline after review. Common mistakes include committing infrequently, committing broken code, or attempting risky manual merges without understanding the history. Best practices include small, frequent commits with clear messages, pushing changes to a remote for backups, and using pull requests for review. Key takeaway: version control preserves work, enables parallel development, and forms a safety net when experiments go wrong. How would your team adopt a simple branching rule for small features?

keyIdea.title: Safety and parallel work
keyIdea.text: VCS prevents data loss, enables parallel feature development, and keeps a complete history of the project.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Version Control
What version control does
  • Records changes and history so you can revert when needed.
  • Allows parallel branches for isolated work on features or fixes.
  • Enables code review workflows to catch errors before merging.
Key takeaway: treat VCS as your project's single source of truth and backup.
Common systems
Git — distributed, branch friendly
Perforce — centralized, handles large binaries
Practice habit: commit frequently with clear messages and push to remote so your work is backed up and shareable.

screens.title: A basic Git workflow you can copy
screens.subtitle: Branch, commit, push, and open a pull request

narration.text: Let's walk through a minimal Git workflow you can use for a single feature. First, create a feature branch to isolate work. This keeps the main line stable while you experiment. Make small, focused commits as you progress — each commit should represent a meaningful step that you could revert if needed. When your feature is ready, push the branch to the remote repository and open a pull request for review. After review and resolving any merge feedback, merge into the main development branch. A concrete example visualizes these commands: create a branch, stage changes, commit, push, then open a pull request. A common misconception is that commits must be perfect; instead, commit often and write clear messages that explain intent. Also avoid committing large generated binaries without locking or using a LFS workflow. Below is a short command sequence you can practice in a test repository. After running these commands, verify your branch appears on the remote and create a pull request in your Git hosting UI. That review step is where teammates catch integration issues and keep history clean. What small commit message would you write for your first change?

keyIdea.title: Small commits, safe merges
keyIdea.text: Isolate work in branches, commit frequently, push to remote, and use pull requests for review before merging.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Git Workflow
Workflow steps
  1. Create a feature branch for your work.
  2. Make incremental changes and commit often with clear messages.
  3. Push the branch to remote and open a pull request for review.
  4. Resolve feedback, then merge into the main development branch.
Misconception: Don't wait to commit until the feature is perfect. Frequent commits are your safety net.
Example commands
git checkout -b new-feature-branch
# make changes
git add .
git commit -m "Implement basic crafting combine logic"
git push origin new-feature-branch
# open a pull request on your remote hosting service
Practice: run these commands in a sandbox repo and open a pull request. Read the diff in your review to understand changes before merging.

screens.title: Version control pitfalls and how to avoid them
screens.subtitle: Frequent errors teams make with VCS and practical fixes

narration.text: Even with a VCS in place, teams can make mistakes that undermine collaboration. One frequent error is committing too rarely, which creates large, hard-to-review patches and increases merge conflicts. The antidote is small, frequent commits with clear messages that explain intent. Another problem is committing broken or untested code to shared branches; protect the mainline by using feature branches and automated checks before merging. Teams also sometimes attempt to resolve complex merge conflicts without first understanding the history; always inspect the commit history and communicate with the author before making risky merges. Binary assets are another challenge: committing large unversioned binaries can bloat the repository. Use a large file storage strategy or Perforce for studios with many big assets. A concrete mitigation plan: require pull requests with at least one reviewer, run automated builds or basic tests on the branch, and use a naming convention for branches so feature scopes are clear. Key takeaway: VCS is powerful, but habits and rules determine whether it protects or undermines your project. Which of these habits would you introduce first on your team?

keyIdea.title: Good habits protect projects
keyIdea.text: Frequent commits, feature branches, reviews, and automation reduce conflicts and preserve history.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › VCS Pitfalls
Common mistakes
  • Committing infrequently — creates large diffs and hard merges.
  • Pushing broken code into shared branches — breaks teammates' work.
  • Resolving merges without understanding history — causes regressions.
  • Storing large binaries directly in Git — repository bloat.
Practical fixes
Commit frequently with clear messages
Use feature branches and pull requests
Require at least one reviewer and run basic checks
Adopt LFS or Perforce for large binaries
Example policy: branch names like feat/crafting-ingredient and PRs labeled with the related sprint number make review and tracking easier.

screens.title: Scope creep: recognition and mitigation
screens.subtitle: How unchecked feature growth derails schedules and budgets

narration.text: Scope creep is the uncontrolled expansion of requirements or features beyond the original plan. In game development, scope creep commonly appears when new mechanics, cosmetic features, or polish requests are added without adjusting timelines or resources. The result is delays, stressed teams, and often unfinished features. Recognizing scope creep early is crucial: signs include an increasing number of high-effort items entering sprints, repeated postponement of core features, or a backlog filled with low-value add-ons. Mitigation strategies begin with a prioritized product backlog driven by impact and feasibility. Use acceptance criteria to define when a story is complete and time-box experiments so exploration doesn't consume implementation hours. Leadership should enforce sprint commitments while allowing urgent blockers to be swapped in under clear rules. Regularly reviewing the game's core vision helps the team say no to lower-impact additions. A practical example: if an artist requests a high-fidelity shader late in development, evaluate its player impact, estimate the added time, and decide whether to move it to a future sprint or fund it with scope adjustment. Key takeaway: treat scope as a resource; every added feature needs time and budget. What rule would your team use to decide whether to accept a late feature request?

keyIdea.title: Control scope
keyIdea.text: Prioritize by impact, time-box experiments, and keep the backlog aligned to the core vision to prevent uncontrolled growth.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Scope Creep
What is scope creep?

Uncontrolled addition of features or requirements that exceed original time and resource estimates, leading to delays and budget overruns.

Signs: frequent late requests, backlog filled with low-impact tasks, core features postponed repeatedly.
Mitigation checklist
  • Prioritize backlog by impact and feasibility.
  • Time-box experiments and prototypes.
  • Require acceptance criteria and estimates for new items.
  • Hold retrospectives to adjust planning and expectations.
Decision rule example: any late request estimated as large must be deferred unless it resolves a critical blocker or has high player impact.

screens.title: Activity: Mini-Scrum Board for a Crafting System
screens.subtitle: Create user stories, break tasks down, and simulate a sprint

narration.text: This activity asks you to lead a tiny sprint for a crafting system. Start by writing 3 to 5 user stories in the format: As a [player], I want [goal], so that [reason]. For example: As a player, I want to combine two basic ingredients to create a potion, so that I can heal my character. For each story break it into smaller tasks and give a rough effort estimate like Small, Medium, or Large. Populate a simple board with three columns: To Do, In Progress, and Done. Then move one or two tasks into In Progress and imagine a daily stand-up: each person states what they did yesterday, what they'll do today, and any blocker. This practice teaches you to turn design intent into actionable tasks, to estimate effort, and to exercise the communication cadence of Scrum. A common mistake is writing overly large user stories that cannot fit in a single sprint; if a story is too big, split it into smaller stories that deliver value independently. After simulating a few days, update the sprint board and reflect: did you over-commit, and what blocked you? That reflection is the core of a retrospective and the primary learning loop in Scrum.

keyIdea.title: Practice sprint planning
keyIdea.text: Breaking stories into tasks and simulating daily stand-ups builds the muscle for realistic sprint planning and communication.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Mini-Scrum Board Activity
Template: Crafting System - Sprint 1
# Crafting System - Sprint 1

## To Do:
* User Story: As a player, I want to combine two basic ingredients to create a potion, so that I can heal my character.
  * Task: Design potion recipe data structure (Effort: Medium)
  * Task: Implement crafting UI wireframe (Effort: Small)
  * Task: Program ingredient combination logic (Effort: Large)
  * Task: Create placeholder potion icon (Effort: Small)

* User Story: As a player, I want to see the crafting recipe for a selected item, so that I know what ingredients I need.
  * Task: Design recipe display UI (Effort: Medium)
  * Task: Program recipe lookup logic (Effort: Large)

## In Progress:
* [Move tasks here as you 'work' on them]

## Done:
* [Move tasks here as you 'complete' them]
Simulate a daily stand-up
Designer: "I finished the recipe fields and will finalize acceptance criteria today. No blockers."
Programmer: "Starting combination logic; I need the data structure confirmed."
Artist: "Placeholder icon ready; will begin high-fidelity art next sprint."
Reflection: After a simulated sprint, ask whether stories delivered player-facing value and whether estimates were realistic.

screens.title: Assessments & common scenarios
screens.subtitle: Practice questions to test your project management skills

narration.text: You should be able to apply these practices in common studio scenarios. Here are two assessment-style prompts you can use to test understanding. First, a team repeatedly overwrites shared assets and loses changes. The correct action is to adopt a version control system and train the team on branching and merge workflows, not just more meetings. Second, during a sprint a critical bug is found in a core mechanic thought to be done. In Scrum, the standard approach is to add the bug to the product backlog and prioritize it, pulling it into a future sprint unless it blocks current sprint goals; immediate team-wide task arrest is usually disruptive unless the bug truly prevents progress. These scenarios highlight the principles: use the right tool for the problem and protect sprint focus while allowing urgent fixes under clear rules. For practice, pick one scenario from your past work and rewrite how you would handle it using the frameworks and tools learned here. That concrete revision often surfaces small changes that dramatically reduce friction in future sprints. Assessments & common scenarios means use scenario-based assessments to verify your understanding of vcs and scrum responses to real issues.. In practical terms, practice questions to test your project management skills. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Test and reflect
keyIdea.text: Use scenario-based assessments to verify your understanding of VCS and Scrum responses to real issues.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Assessment Scenarios
Scenario 1 — Overwritten assets
Problem: Team members accidentally overwrite each other's files. Correct response: adopt a VCS, define branch rules, and train the team in commits, pushes, and pull requests.
Assessment question: Which practice most directly prevents overwritten work? (Answer: Version control system)
Scenario 2 — Critical bug mid-sprint
Problem: A core mechanic fails after testing. Correct response: triage the bug and add it to the backlog for prioritization. If it blocks sprint goals, swap tasks; otherwise schedule in the next sprint.
Assessment question: Should you stop the sprint immediately for every bug? No — only for bugs that block current sprint progress.

narration.text: Let's consolidate the essential ideas. First, Agile methodologies, and Scrum in particular, are generally better suited for game development than linear Waterfall approaches because they embrace iteration and player feedback. Second, clearly defined roles — Producer, Lead Designer, Leads for programming and art, and QA — ensure ownership and smooth handoffs. Third, practical project artifacts like sprint boards, burndown charts, and Gantt views answer different planning questions: use boards for daily flow, burndowns for sprint health, and Gantt for milestone dependencies. Fourth, version control is non-negotiable for collaboration: branch per feature, commit frequently, push to a remote, and use pull requests for review. Fifth, manage scope proactively with prioritized backlogs, acceptance criteria, and time-boxed experiments. These concepts fit together: a prioritized backlog feeds sprints, clear roles execute tasks, visuals monitor progress, and VCS protects the work. Carry this compact framework into your next feature planning session and test one change: add branch rules, update your board daily, or hold a short retrospective. Which single change will you try first?

narration.text: Keep three quick rules in mind as you manage game projects. Rule one: prefer iterative workflows like Scrum for creative, changeable work because they let you learn from play and reduce rework. Rule two: always use version control and a clear branching policy so parallel work doesn't overwrite itself and the project history remains recoverable. Rule three: limit scope creep by prioritizing the backlog, time-boxing experiments, and enforcing acceptance criteria. These short rules are practical checks you can run anytime planning or feature requests threaten to stretch your schedule.
